https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Lev Shlosberg said he was punished for his political position By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 2 hours ago Russia's prominent anti-war politician Lev Shlosberg has been sentenced to 11 years and one month in a penal colony for "discrediting" the country's armed forces and "spreading false information" about them. Shlosberg, 63, condemned the verdict by a court in the city of Pskov, saying its only task was to "punish a person for his political, public and civil position". His liberal political party Yabloko, which he is deputy head of, said it would appeal. The ruling came just minutes before Russia's Supreme Court rejected Yabloko's appeal against a ban on it taking part in September's parliamentary elections. Yabloko was the only registered party to oppose Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched in 2022. Since the start of the invasion, any remaining opposition in Russia to President Vladimir Putin - who has been in power for nearly 27 years - has been crushed. Public shows of dissent have been suppressed by wartime censorship laws and can trigger hefty fines or long prison sentences. Figure caption, What we know about anti-war party banned from election in Russia The court in Pskov, north-western Russia, delivered its verdict on Monday. It found Shlosberg guilty of "public actions aimed at discrediting the use of the armed forces of the Russian Federation". The prosecution had demanded 12 years and one month in jail. The criminal charges were brought following Shlosberg's comments published on social media. In his closing speech, Shlosberg again rejected all the charges, describing the trial as "an imitation of an investigation" in order to "achieve an obviously illegal goal", according to a transcript published by the Novaya Gazeta newspaper. The opposition politician also repeated his call for a ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine war and the start of a "political dialogue". He was repeatedly interrupted by the presiding judge. Yabloko was struck off the ballots earlier this month over accusations that the party publicly supports the "international LGBT movement", which Russia's Supreme Court designates as extremist. A lawsuit brought forward by pro-Kremlin nationalist party Rodina also argued that Yabloko was guilty of copyright infringement. Yabloko rejects all the accusations. All 10 other parties taking part in the 18-20 September election support the war in Ukraine. The latest ratings of the ruling United Russia slipped to 32.1% earlier this month - the lowest figure since May, according to Russia's state-owned pollster VCIOM. Still, the Kremlin is widely believed to have the resources to deliver the outcome it wants at the election. Independent election watchdogs have been deprived of much of their ability to monitor and challenge the process. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Demonstrators at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on Monday to protest against the rise of the far-right AfD party. Photograph: T Seeliger/ hutterstock View image in fullscreen Demonstrators at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on Monday to protest against the rise of the far-right AfD party. Photograph: T Seeliger/ hutterstock Germany Firewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’? Many fear chancellor is wrong man for the job at a time when Germany’s defences against far right are crumbling Deborah Cole in Berlin Sat 12 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection of Germany ’s joyous reunification three decades ago, and a threat to the democratic postwar order. Sizing up the repercussions of last weekend’s win for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, German commentators expressed a sense of doom, panic and helplessness in the political establishment. With nearly 44% of the vote, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its media savvy chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is racing to find enough support from the other parties to prop up what would be the first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period. View image in fullscreen AfD co-leaders Alice Weidel (right) and Tino Chrupalla (left) with Saxony-Anhalt lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP It is still anyone’s guess whether he will succeed, leaving a corrosive uncertainty at the heart of Europe’s top economic power. Hanging in the balance is the fate of Friedrich Merz’s centre-right government, once called “ democracy’s last shot ” to prevent an extremist takeover in Germany. ‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capital Read more The result in Saxony-Anhalt has put the conservative chancellor on the ropes, with further punishment for his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) expected in two more state polls later this month . “This is the worst defeat for the CDU in years – decades – and something has changed, not just in Saxony-Anhalt but in all of Germany ,” he said on Monday. Whether or not he survives politically until the next general election, due in 2029, will have dramatic repercussions for Germany and its European allies trying to beat back anti-democratic forces. Pivotal elections are due next year in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Poland. Merz’s many critics say the 70-year-old former BlackRock executive is the wrong man at such a consequential crossroads, calling him a ham-fisted and empathetically challenged leader who is erratic in his messaging . Only in office 16 months, the chancellor often seemed incapable of one of the basic tasks of leadership: making the case to voters that accepting bitter pills now could lead to a brighter future, said the political scientist Thomas Biebricher of Frankfurt’s Goethe University. View image in fullscreen Friedrich Merz: his future as chancellor is uncertain. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images “The prevailing impression at the moment is that, in terms of communication, he is unable to explain the many reforms – and the sacrifices they entail – to the public, and thereby win their acceptance,” Biebricher said, referring to planned cuts to the statutory pension and healthcare schemes . The former chancellor Angela Merkel , Merz’s longtime rival within the CDU, has criticised him publicly for his hardline rhetoric on migration and integration but said she took no pleasure in the debacle given the stakes. “This is a turning point – a real turning point – in the history of the federal republic of Germany,” said Merkel, who left office of her own accord in 2021 after 16 years in power. “As a CDU member it breaks my heart.” View image in fullscreen Merz speaking to Angela Merkel at the CDU federal conference in Stuttgart in February. Photograph: Getty Images Speaking at a digital affairs conference on Tuesday, she advised Merz to rethink his messaging in a changing political ecosystem in which emotions counted more than facts. Merkel, 72, noted that the CDU had pointed to data during the Saxony-Anhalt campaign showing that joblessness had fallen and household wealth had risen in the small, relatively poor state. “And then [Siegmund] says: ‘That may be so, but that’s not how it feels.’” The AfD formed in 2013, during Merkel’s tenure, as a Eurosceptic outfit opposed to bailouts for debt-mired countries. It grew increasingly radical during the 2015-2016 refugee influx , when she left the borders open to more than a million asylum seekers fleeing war and hardship. Merz took office last year saying he would put the country back on track after the implosion of the previous government under Olaf Scholz . He promised a return to economic growth, a restoration of defence capabilities and urgent repairs to the creaking social welfare system. His recipe for confronting the far right – one of his key pledges – was competence in governing and solutions for Germans’ most urgent problems. Merz also promised a rejection of Merkel’s open-border policy in an attempt to rob the AfD of its signature issue. He had infamously accepted support from the far-right party for a tough draft law on migration just before the February 2025 general election, before back-pedalling in the face of protests. View image in fullscreen AfD co-leader Alice Weidel walks past Merz at the Bundestag this week. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images As “irregular” arrivals of migrants have fallen sharply since Merz took office, the AfD has successfully pivoted to a broader range of concerns about deindustrialisation, regional identity, affordability and crime to gain ground far beyond its eastern heartland. The AfD, widely seen as more radical than comparable European parties, had been relegated to permanent opposition in Germany by the “firewall” strategy of shunning by the mainstream parties. But this policy is now widely seen to have failed, allowing the AfD to snipe from the sidelines about the slow pace of any positive change. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Biebricher said that for all Merz’s weaknesses, replacing him would not be a magic bullet for the mountain of challenges facing German security and prosperity. View image in fullscreen A forensic technician works near a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig airport, where a drone with an explosive device was found last month. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP As well as the threat from Russia , he cited decrepit infrastructure, the demographic crunch on social welfare benefits, competition from China in once mighty industries such as car manufacturing , and geopolitical upheaval weighing on supply chains and energy imports. “None of that simply goes away the moment you have someone who communicates better,” Biebricher told public radio . View image in fullscreen Volkswagen employees during a rally against mass job cut plans in Zwickau in July. Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty Images Merz’s centre-right CDU-CSU bloc, divided between conservatives and moderates, is nevertheless known for its internal discipline in times of crisis – if only out of fear of even graver consequences from drastic changes. The situation is seen as so grim that it has triggered paralysis, with neither the popular North Rhine-Westphalia state premier, Hendrik Wüst, or Bavaria’s ambitious leader, Markus Söder, keen at this stage to snatch the poisoned chalice. “Merz has now reached a stage where the crisis – which he himself constantly exacerbates – is stabilising him,” said the veteran political journalist Bernd Ulrich of Die Zeit newspaper . “The CDU and the government (in coalition with the Social Democrats) as a whole are in such a dire state that, as far as anyone can tell, no one wants to take over his post.” Wüst, 51, leads a coalition with the Greens in Germany’s most populous state and faces a re-election battle next April. If he wins, the calls for Merz to make way for him may grow louder. Söder, who represents the bloc’s conservative wing, shares Merz’s view that it needs to echo the AfD’s harsh rhetoric on migration in order to win back support – a strategy political scientists have long disparaged as counterproductive. 1:24 ‘We should have learned more from history’: Germans react to AfD win – video Yet the dangers of keeping a revolt at bay by betting on a status quo voters so clearly reject are apparent. Much will depend on how bad the news is from the regional elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on 20 September. The AfD is polling well in both states, with clear momentum after Saxony-Anhalt, putting pressure on the CDU in particular. During a fiery clash with the AfD in parliament this week in which he laid out the threat it poses to German democracy , Merz was reflective about how to steer the country – and himself – out of the current straits. He quoted from a letter he received from the rector of a theological university arguing how many opportunities still lay ahead for Germany and advising him not to give in to despair. Merz said he intended to take this to heart and stay on as chancellor using a new roadmap: “Admit mistakes, forgive, get back on your feet, shape the future.” Explore more on these topics Germany Europe Friedrich Merz Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) The far right Angela Merkel Migration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.wearemoviegeeks.com/tag/1990.text: Well, that’s a coincidence. This last weekend of Summer sees another feature film with its roots in Children’s TV pop culture. While the Looney Tunes crew originated as short subjects in movie theatres, when TV arrived, these seven-minute epics had a long-time Saturday morning slot on network TV, while being part of the content for many local “kiddie shows” hosted usually by members of the “news team” (in my area, the longest airing was “Cactus Pete”). This other flick explores the world of puppet shows and other “live-action” programs centering on actors in big puffy costumes that were a staple on “edu-tainment” programs, usually on weekday afternoons on PBS affiliates. Oh, the other big difference between these two movies is that the other one is a satirical comedy while this one is almost purely parody-horror. Yes, you read that right. And, like many other horror icons like Michael, Jason, and Freddy, he’s also best known by his first name. It’s BUDDY. Oh, and that’s the name of the TV program, “It’s Buddy”.The film’s first moments are the show’s opening titles, introducing the energetic preteen human children cavorting with a six-foot-tall plush orange unicorn. In this bright, shiny pastel-colored world, everything seems to be alive, from the mailbox to the furniture, and even a backpack named “Strappy” that belongs to a young girl named Freddy (Delaney Quinn). There are also some “peripheral adult” humans like Mailman Miles and Nurse Nancy. However, the main”players” are Freddy and her pre-teen pals Wade, Oliver, and Josh. Oh, Buddy is their fuzzy lil’ toy that comes to life and “life-sized” (voiced by Keegan-Michael Key) when the kids speak his name. In this episode, the kids are throwing a big “dance party”, which excites everyone except for the surly (maybe he’s edging closer to being a teen) Josh, who would rather read his SF book. Buddy takes him aside and tries to gently prod him into some dance moves. When Josh balks, Buddy pushes him “off-camera”. On the next episode, there’s a new character in the opening, Hannah. When Freddy and Wade ask Buddy about Josh, Buddy tells them that he’s gone to “Diamond City”. Later, Freddy spies Josh’s book in “Trashy”. And when they see Buddy with Nurse Nancy, the kids know that something is very wrong. Can they escape Buddy’s “slay ground”?The story then switches to the “real world”, as a busy mother, Grace (Cristin Miloti), begins to unravel as she has flashes of a different reality. This concerns her hubby Ben (Topher Grace) and her two sons. These dark thoughts culminate when the TV pops on to reveal a beckoning Buddy, an image Ben doesn’t see. And there’s nothing about this show online. Can she, along with Freddy and her pals, escape the warm, lingering long hugs from this orange “play(slay)mate”? Most of the heavy human “dramatics’ are handled by two actresses. The one in “reality ” is the talented Ms. Milioti (so wonderful in the HBO limited series “The Penguin”) as the distraught and extremely confused Grace. She is a “woman on the edge” and Milioti draws us into her fearful realizations, while also venting her frustrations when being casually dismissed. In the TV world, it’s Quinn as the increasingly frightened Freddy. She’s the first to see that all is not “sweetness and fun” in their backyard setting. Yet Quinn gives her an inner strength and intelligence that keeps us in her “corner”. Topher Grace uses her sitcom-honed comic timing as Ben tries to understand and stifle this “disruption”. Without spoiling this inspired casting, another one of the trapped humans is played by a cult TV fave who’s a beloved star’s sibling (hint hint). And his fellow traveler is a snarky puppet voiced by a two-time Oscar-nominated actor. But the best vocal performance is Key in the title role (with Sergey Zhuravsky in the big suit), who switches from an all-too-sweet “sing-song” cadence to threatening passive-aggressive menace that is quite chilling. Much like this year’s big hits OBSESSION and BACKROOMS, this is “high concept horror” on a grand scale, orchestrated by another filmmaker from the online short film arena. Casper Kelly made a big splash with his remarkable 80’s sitcom spoof TOO MANY COOKS a dozen years ago, so he was more than adequately prepared for this deep, deep dive in 1990’s kids’ TV. Crafting the screenplay with Jamie King, they capture the brightly lit, candy-colored fakery of that era, mixing elements of “Pee Wee’s Playhouse”, “Thomas the Tank Engine”, and, well, let’s call him “Purple-saurus Rex”, complete with a quartet of kids a bit too mature for the show’s intended audience. So they have the “look” down pat, but is this an SNL-style TV spoof skit that’s stretched too thin for a feature? This is a fairly brisk 96 minutes, helped by the jumps between the “TV world” and the “real”. And there’s a sustained creepy vibe, heightened by the artificiality of the settings, especially the songs and “hi-jinks”. And, as the online ads promise, it is gory, more than earning its “R” rating, though that is exaggerated to excess. Kudos to the use of practical effects, though some CGI is used sparingly. Kelly and King’s script takes several interesting and unexpected twists and turns that lead to a finale that inspires a deeper dive to explore the hints of a dark, sinister conspiracy. Sure, making fun of that old 90s PBS saccharine slob is an easy target, but there are enough scares, shocks, and gags (in every sense) to warrant a big warm cinema hug for our new movie pal BUDDY. Just remember to smile and do what he says…or else. 3 out of 4 BUDDY is now playing exclusively in theatres Share this: Post Share on Threads (Opens in new window) Threads Now, just two weeks ago, I reviewed the rare movie hybrid, a sports/horror flick called HIM. As it nears the end of its deservedly brief theatrical run, another sports film hits the multiplex. However, its subgenre is one that is most familiar in cinema history, the sports “biopic”. To be even more specific, this is a dramatic profile of a fighter. If you’re thinking about pugilists like LaMotta (of RAGING BULL) fame or Muhammad Ali, then you’re in a different arena. No, this week’s new release is set in the world of MMA (Mixed Martial Arts), a backdrop in action flicks going way back to 1980’s THE OCTAGAN. In more recent years, diverse actors, from Kevin James to Halle Berry, have flexed their fists and feet on the canvas. Now an action flick superstar, who first gained fame in another fighting ring, gets a chance to show off his dramatic skills (along with his impressive pecs) as the athlete dubbed (in an acclaimed HBO documentary) THE SMASHING MACHINE. Yes, that’s the intimidating nickname of Mark Kerr (Dwayne Johnson). We’re first introduced to him as he’s being interviewed at a UFC match in the late 1990s. The undefeated champ is asked how he’d feel if he lost a match. It’s something he’s never thought about, so he’s truly at a loss for words. Later, after another victory, we observe him grabbing an extra vial or two of painkillers. Luckily, he can’t hide it from his devoted but often annoyed (Mark doesn’t “open up”) girlfriend, Dawn (Emily Blunt). In search of bigger cash prizes, Kerr joins, along with old wrestling pal and trainer Mark Coleman (Ryan Bader), the rival UFC league in Japan, PRIDE. Ultimately, Kerr’s substance abuse takes its toll as he loses focus in the ring, with one big bout ending as “No Contest”. Finally he enters a rehab facility as Coleman’s star begins to rise as a solo MMA star. When Kerr completes the “program,” his sobriety puts an even greater strain on his relationship with Dawn. But he’s still a big draw at PRIDE, so Kerr is back at the training gym, guided by his mentor Bas Rutten (himself). But will the strain of addiction, paired with a chaotic home life derail his chances at a big championship event that could have him facing his old buddy Coleman? The film truly rests on those (really, really big and broad) shoulders of Johnson, who utilizes his considerable charm and charisma, which propelled him on the big screen, making us believe him as this worldwide champion. And then he surprises (he’s “gone A24”) us by plunging into the darkness of this “sporting life”, showing us how the affable Kerr “cons’ the medical system with his infectious grin and “gentle giant” persona. Kudos to Johnson for getting out his “comfort zone” of the overblown action “tentpoles” (in some of them he looked a tad “unconnected”, to the point of “phoning it in”) to explore the psyche of the laser-focused competitor. Perhaps he’s at his best early on as Kerr describes the “rush” of delivering a knockout blow. Matching him in intensity is the versatile Ms. Blunt, who makes Dawn more than Kerr’s “eye candy” housemate, and keeps us “off kilter” as she lashes out over being on the “sidelines” and viewed by her beau’s team as a flitting “distraction” from battle. By the big “blow-up” in the third act, Blunt makes her a volatile “wild card’ in a verbal (and nearly physical) throw down reminicent of Albee’s George and Martha. In his first acting gig, Bader is very compelling as “friend to the end” Coleman, making us wish for a greater “dive” into his story, aside from a few brief minutes of him playing with his adorable offspring. Also solid is Rutten as, well, Bas Rutten, a tough but nurturing guru for Kerr, in and out of the ring. Much like the creative parting of the Coen brothers, this is the first film from writer/director Benny Safdie after a long cinematic collaboration with brother Josh. And as I noted, he turns Johnson and Blunt into a potent screen team (we know her dramatic chops, but he’s doing a big career shift). It’s a shame that they’re not in service to a more compelling script. Focusing on three or four years in Kerr’s “sports rise”, we don’t get a chance to see him in his “hungry years” during the “climb”. In other ways, the story needs more ‘space”. We only see him enter and exit the rehab center, with no scenes of his “steps”. And often Kerr is so stoic, it makes us wonder what his motivations are (especially when he’s fixated on a demolition derby match), though it gives us a chance to appreciate the subtle, but superb make-up work of Kazu Hiro, chipping away at “the Rock”. Plus, the film’s pacing somewhat “lurches” from interchangeable matches (it’s often difficult to ID the fighters as they become “pretzels”) to another screaming match at the Kerr casa in Phoenix. The often overbearing (drowning out dialogue) music score (two ill-timed Elvis tunes and a “jackhammer” jazz drum solo during the big matches) doesn’t aid the film. Yes, there are a few interesting sequences, particularly when Kerr sweetly explains his job to a grandma in a doctor’s waiting area, or when he takes his pal to “press the flesh” with his Tokyo fans, but the script feels like it’s “spinning its wheels” until the big “updates” prior to the end titles. Fans of the two principals will be pleased with their taut performances, but many will find that there are more than a few hints of “rust” and strain in THE SMAHING MACHINE. 2 Out of 4 THE SMASHING MACHINES opens in theatres everywhere on Friday, October 3, 2025 Share this: Post Share on Threads (Opens in new window) Threads And now I believe we’re officially in the Fall movie season, as the newest project from one of the most acclaimed “indie” filmmakers of the last twenty-five years or so releases his newest work into theatres, not just in the “art house” cinemas, but in multiplexes everywhere (and maybe a few drive-ins). That’s because it’s a much more general audience “accessible” than many of his previous projects. For one thing, it boasts a stellar cast headed by a “rising star”. And it’s in the “area” of one of the most popular genres, one that’s usually abundant in the summertime, the “crime thriller”, mixed with a few quirky comedy touches. It’s based on a popular novel, actually part of a “series” whose “double meaning” title becomes apparent while watching CAUGHT STEALING. After a bright and sunny prologue at the final moments of a big high school baseball game, we’re sent to the grimy Lower East Side streets of NYC circa 1998. Twenty-something Hank Thompson (Austin Butler) has a pretty great life “slingin’ suds” at a rowdy “dive bar”. The best part of his gig is “last call” when his gorgeous EMT girlfriend Yvonne (Zo Kravits) waits for him to lock up. From there, the duo heads to his grungy walk-up apartment. In the hallway, they run into Hank’s punk-rocker (mohawk and spiked leather jacket, natch’) Brit neighbor, Russ (Matt Smith). He’s gotta’ fly home to see his dying Dad, so he asks Hank to take care of his cat, Bud. No prob. After some “sexytime”, Yvonne leaves for work in the morning as Hank nurses one of many nasty hangovers. Seems he’s trying to numb the pain of a painful memory. A call to his mother in Patterson, CA eases his head as they bond over a love of the San Francisco Giants baseball team. Later, he accosts two tough-looking Russians trying to break into Russ’s place. The thugs think that Russ gave Hank something they want. He tells them that he has nothing aside from Bud the cat, which earns Hank a severe beating from the two. Waking up in a hospital bed, he tells Yvonne that he can’t wait to be discharged. Back at his place, Hank is interviewed by Narcotics Detective Roman (Regina King), who informs him that Russ is into some shady business with the Russian mob, and he’s also involved with two “scary monsters”, the vicious Hasidic Drucker brothers (Liev Schreiber and Vincent D’Onofrio). After they leave, Hank uncovers a key that Russ left. He heads back to the bar to hide it, but begins a “bender” that leaves him unable to recall what he did with it. This doesn’t sit well with the Russians, who return with their equally violent boss, a Puerto Rican club owner named Colorado (Benito A Martinez Ocasio, AKA pop music superstar “Bad Bunny”). Can Hank escape them as he tries to cut through the drunken fog of the previous night? And if he does lose them, what will happen if the Drucker brothers catch up to him? And when will that darn Russ return? That rising star I mentioned earlier would be the very charismatic Mr. Butler, who is steadily building an interesting movie resume after his breakthrough as Elvis. He is the reluctant hero with roots in classic noir cinema. Hank is a fairly good guy who is plunged into the dark netherworld of 90s drug gangs. But he’s not without his own darkness. Butler shows Hank’s inner torment as he wakes up from memories of a not-so-long-ago time when his poor judgment took away everything from him. But there’s little time for pity, or for boozy amnesia, as the walls close in. Through his expressive eyes, Butler shows us how Hank must drink in his new situations while formulating a plan at near light speed. He’s also terrific in the lighter moments, especially in the crazy, flirty chemistry-fueled scenes with the bubbly Kravitz as his sexy voice of reason, Yvonne. She truly cares about Hank, which exacerbates her frustration with his lifestyle choices, revved up after that hospital stay was cut short. Another calming influence is King, whose tough but still tender cop may be just the guide to get Hank past this nightmare alive. Smith brings some angry, funny energy as the Cockney rocker who fights to keep his 80s style while adoring his kitty. Schreiber and D’Onofrio are very compelling as the brothers whose religious adherence and attire juxtapose with their murderous intent and ruthlessness. They seem reasonable at times, until they see an opportunity to strike with deadly force. At least they’re sweet with their Bubbe, played by the always endearing Carol Kane as the stern and nurturing matriarch, though there’s a touch of menace in the advice she offers to Hank. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c962.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy By James Landale Diplomatic correspondent ,Â Reporting from Jerusalem Published 17 October 2026 Updated 2 hours ago A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating. But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel". The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look". It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law". In Saturday's incident the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah. They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest. Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown. The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle. Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice. "Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said. "As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. "Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them." Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved. But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security." The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters." "According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux, the left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack. It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility". A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible." It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge". Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence. The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground. "It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged." "The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said. The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Panoramice » Society Today » „The platform is down: many foreign workers left without residence rights “The platform is down: many foreign workers left without residence rights In April, the Romanian Government adopted a new ordinance regarding the recruitment and placement of foreign workers, following months of negotiations with stakeholders across society. WorkinRomania.gov.ro Iulia Hau , 14.10.2026, 14:00 Although the ordinance entered into force on April 27, the hiring of foreigners is practically blocked: the WorkinRomania platform has not been functioning since August 15—meaning for nearly seven weeks. Hundreds, perhaps thousands, of foreigners thus risk losing their right of residency. Georgiana Bădescu, coordinator of the Migration and Asylum Program at the Legal Resources Center, explains where the deadlock stems from. “Now, unfortunately, we are in an abyss when it comes to putting the provisions of the ordinance into practice. The WorkinRomania platform is blocked due to a lawsuit at the Court of Appeal regarding the suspension of the order on the list of deficit occupations, the case being between the Employers’ Organization of Labor Importers and the Ministry of Labor.” PIFM is the acronym for the Employers’ Organization of Labor Importers ( Patronatul Importatorilor de Forță de Muncă ), the organization that requested a court-ordered suspension of the list of deficit occupations. The list included 289 professions. The organization considers it an abusive restriction because it limits the professions for which foreign workers can be brought in. Their argument: the Ministry supposedly chose the professions restrictively, without a real market analysis, affecting companies’ right to recruit according to actual market needs. Georgiana Bădescu continues: “Due to this suspension obtained by PIFM in court, the WorkinRomania platform has been blocked since August 15. Where does this situation leave us? It severely affects every migrant worker, because there are multiple situations where a migrant worker has entered, will enter, or is entering—as we speak—into involuntary illegal residency, due to these bureaucratic problems, due to this lawsuit, and because there are no guarantees regarding their rights. Persons whose documents will expire—and here I am referring to the residency permit, which can expire at any time—I am referring to the 90-day period granted to foreigners to change their employer, I am referring to those who arrived with a work visa whom the first employer no longer wants, because we also have this situation—all these people will enter illegal residency through no fault of their own, without any kind of guarantee, and without any extension of their right of residency existing.” The problem of migrants ending up in illegal residency through no fault of their own is not new. The press in Romania and abroad, as well as human rights organizations, have pointed this out repeatedly. To respond to this issue, the Government ran a two-month regularization program this year for migrants in this situation. Following it, 3,666 people regained their legal residency rights, and 112 were forced to leave the country because they did not meet the conditions for enrollment in the program. Experts believe that the number of people who presented themselves during the program was small compared to the actual number of potential beneficiaries. They say many migrants did not come forward out of fear that they wouldn’t qualify and would risk being forcibly returned to their countries of origin. Georgiana Bădescu, from the Legal Resources Center, points out: “The timeframes are such that they place the migrant in a situation of involuntary, non-attributable illegal stay; consequently, the Romanian legislator needs to step in and provide certain guarantees. The only thing we have secured so far is a statement from the General Inspectorate for Immigration which assures us that the principle of proportionality will be applied when examining each individual case, but that is far from sufficient. At present, if a migrant falls into a state of illegal stay due to bureaucratic bottlenecks and court proceedings, and is then stopped on the street, he or she will be issued a return decision and will be forced to leave for their country of origin. We are talking about people with loans, people acting in good faith, individuals who have held legal residency in Romania for over four years and who will find themselves in a state of illegal stay simply because the online platform isn’t working. So we are entitled to ask: where is the proportionality? Where is the respect for migrants’ rights? Because, in this situation, a violation of their rights is clearly taking place.” The Center for Legal Resources has addressed a public letter to the Ministries of Internal Affairs and Labor, the General Inspectorate for Immigration, and the National Employment Agency, calling for the system to be adapted to the current situation and for guarantees to be provided to foreign nationals. At the same time, Georgiana Bădescu criticizes certain amendments made to the ordinance by the Chamber of Deputies’ Labor Committee, arguing that they contradict the very reasons for which the ordinance was adopted. “The Labor Committee’s amendments concern fees imposed exclusively on foreigners, a provision that is discriminatory in itself, because you cannot single out a foreign worker for a fee based expressly on their foreign status as opposed to a Romanian employee; I am referring to the fact that this leaves loopholes for agencies and employers to charge fees to migrants, as any such loophole allows an agency to continue charging the worker. This wording regarding ‘consultancy fees’ will be exploited by the private sector, we know this from both past and present experience, as there are already instances where agencies demand fees from migrants, as well as the security deposit payable to the state. They do not want to keep the provision requiring wages to be paid exclusively via bank card.” Paying wages exclusively via bank card would be a significant guarantee for migrants, she explains. It would help prove unpaid wages in labor disputes. This is particularly important because few migrants can afford a lawyer to represent them in court. https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: With 0.56% support, Te Pāti Māori will be stoked with its result tonight, writes Jamie Tahana. It seems odd, but the Māori party has spent the election deliberately asking people not to give them their party vote. Instead, they asked for electorate votes only. Just a reminder, seven of the seats in New Zealand’s parliament are reserved for representatives of Māori voters – you can read more about them here. The party’s co-leaders, Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, have comfortably won their respective seats of Waiariki and Te Tai Hauauru; Oriini Kaipara swept the Auckland seat of Tamaki Makaurau; Hana Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, who hit international stardom for her haka in parliament, has cruised across the line in Hauraki-Waikato; while Aperahama Edwards holds a narrow lead over the Greens’ Hūhana Lydon in the far North seat of Te Tai Tokerau.
